notes.summary:
This topic is about how data is collected, sorted into classes and shown in tables, diagrams and graphs. Paper 2 asks 6 to 10 questions here. Most are direct definitions (primary or secondary data, questionnaire or schedule, kinds of classification) and short calculations: class mark, class boundaries, class width, pie-chart angles, histogram heights for unequal classes and ogives.

Learn the vocabulary first, then practise the four small calculations: class mark, boundaries, pie angle and adjusted frequency.

concepts.title: What statistics and data mean
concepts.body:
Statistics (plural sense) means numerical facts collected for a purpose, such as the population of each state. Statistics (singular sense) means the methods of collecting, organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting such facts.

  • A single value (one student's marks) is not "statistics". Statistics are aggregates of facts.
  • Population (universe): every unit we want to study. Sample: the part we actually study.
  • Variable: a measurable characteristic (height, income). Attribute: a quality that cannot be measured, only counted (gender, literacy, colour).
  • Discrete variable takes separate values, usually counts (number of children: 0, 1, 2). Continuous variable can take any value in a range (height 160.4 cm).

concepts.title: Scales of measurement
concepts.body:
ScaleWhat it allowsExample
NominalNames or labels only; no orderBlood group, religion, jersey number
OrdinalOrder, but gaps are not equalRanks in a race, grades A, B, C
IntervalEqual gaps, but no true zeroTemperature in °C, calendar years
RatioEqual gaps and a true zero, so ratios make senseHeight, weight, income, age

Mode suits nominal data, median suits ordinal data, and the mean needs interval or ratio data.

concepts.title: Primary and secondary data
concepts.body:
• Primary data are collected for the first time by the investigator for the purpose in hand. They are original, more reliable for that purpose, but cost more time and money.
  • Secondary data were already collected by someone else and are reused, for example Census reports, RBI bulletins, NSO reports, journals.
  • Data are primary for the agency that collects them and secondary for everyone who later uses them.
  • Before using secondary data, check that they are reliable, suitable for your purpose and adequate.

Published sources: government publications, reports of committees, international bodies (UN, IMF), journals. Unpublished sources: records kept by offices, research workers and firms.

concepts.title: Methods of collecting primary data
concepts.body:
MethodHow it worksGood for
Direct personal investigationThe investigator meets every informant himselfSmall, local, confidential enquiries
Indirect oral investigationInformation is taken from third persons (witnesses) who know the factsEnquiry committees, when informants will not talk
Information through local agents or correspondentsLocal agents send information regularlyNewspapers, crop estimates; quick but less accurate
Mailed questionnaireA list of questions is posted; the informant fills it inWide area, educated informants; cheap but low response
Schedules through enumeratorsTrained enumerators ask the questions and fill in the form themselvesLarge enquiries like the Census; works with illiterate informants

Questionnaire = filled in by the informant. Schedule = filled in by the enumerator after asking the informant. A good questionnaire is short, uses simple questions, avoids personal or leading questions, and asks questions in a logical order.

Census (complete enumeration) studies every unit. Sample survey studies only some units. A pilot survey is a small trial run to test the questionnaire.

concepts.title: Classification of data
concepts.body:
Classification is arranging data into groups by common features. It is the first step after collection.

BasisNameExample
PlaceGeographical (spatial)Wheat output by state
TimeChronological (temporal)India's population 1951 to 2011
Quality / attributeQualitativePeople by literacy or gender
Size / measurementQuantitativeStudents by marks or height
  • Simple (dichotomous) classification: one attribute, two classes (literate or illiterate).
  • Manifold classification: several attributes at once (gender, then literacy within each gender).
  • Data arranged by time form a time series.

concepts.title: Tabulation
concepts.body:
A table arranges classified data in rows and columns. Parts of a table, from top to bottom:

  1. Table number and title (what, where, when).
  2. Head note (units, such as "in ₹ crore").
  3. Captions: column headings. Stubs: row headings.
  4. Body: the figures.
  5. Foot note (explains a figure) and source note (where the data came from).

A simple (one-way) table shows one characteristic; a two-way table shows two; a manifold table shows more. A general purpose (reference) table keeps all data for reference; a special purpose (summary) table is made for one analysis.

concepts.title: Frequency distribution words
concepts.body:
Take the classes 10–20, 20–30, 30–40 with frequencies 4, 9, 7.

TermMeaningFor 20–30
Class limitsThe two end values writtenLower 20, upper 30
Class width (size, interval)Upper boundary − lower boundary10
Class mark (mid-value)(Lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 225
FrequencyNumber of values in the class9
Relative frequencyFrequency ÷ total frequency9/20 = 0.45
Less-than cumulative frequencyFrequencies added from the top4 + 9 = 13
Frequency densityFrequency ÷ class width0.9
  • Exclusive method (10–20, 20–30): the upper limit is not included in the class, so 20 goes into 20–30. Limits and boundaries are the same.
  • Inclusive method (10–19, 20–29): both limits are included. To get class boundaries, find the gap (20 − 19 = 1), take half (0.5), subtract it from lower limits and add it to upper limits: 9.5–19.5, 19.5–29.5.
  • Open-end class: "below 10" or "60 and above".
  • Sturges' rule for number of classes: k = 1 + 3.322 log10 N. For N = 100, k = 1 + 6.644 ≈ 8. Class width ≈ range ÷ k.

concepts.title: Diagrams
concepts.body:
Diagrams give a quick visual comparison; they are not exact.

  • Simple bar diagram: one bar per item; only the length matters, widths are equal.
  • Multiple (grouped) bar diagram: bars side by side to compare two or more series (exports and imports each year).
  • Subdivided (component) bar diagram: one bar split into parts. Percentage bar diagram: every bar is 100 and parts are percentages.
  • Deviation bar: shows positive and negative values (profit and loss).
  • Pie chart: a circle cut into sectors. Angle of a part = (value of part ÷ total) × 360°. A part that is 25% gets 90°.
  • Pictograms use pictures; cartograms use maps.
  • Bar diagrams are one-dimensional; rectangles, squares and circles drawn by area are two-dimensional; cubes and cylinders are three-dimensional.

Mini example: monthly expense ₹2,400, rent ₹600. Rent's angle = 600/2400 × 360° = 90°.

concepts.title: Graphs of a frequency distribution
concepts.body:
• Histogram: touching rectangles over class boundaries. The area of each bar shows the frequency. When classes have unequal widths, use height = frequency × (standard width ÷ actual width). Mode can be found from a histogram.
  • Frequency polygon: join the mid-points of the tops of histogram bars (or plot class marks against frequencies) and close it at both ends on the x-axis. Its area equals the histogram's area.
  • Frequency curve: a smooth freehand curve through the polygon's points.
  • Ogive (cumulative frequency curve): the less-than ogive plots less-than cf against upper boundaries and rises; the more-than ogive plots more-than cf against lower boundaries and falls. The two ogives cross at the median. Quartiles, deciles and percentiles are read from an ogive.
  • Lorenz curve: shows inequality of income or wealth; the further it bends from the line of equal distribution, the greater the inequality.
  • A histogram cannot be drawn for open-end classes without closing them; a line graph or historigram is used for time series.

varieties.name: Data sources and collection methods
varieties.how: Ask two things: who collected the data first (you or someone else), and who fills in the form (informant = questionnaire, enumerator = schedule).

example.q: Data taken from the Census report by a researcher for his study are:
steps: The Census office collected these data first, for its own purpose.
The researcher is reusing data collected by someone else.
Reused data are secondary data for the user.

varieties.name: Classification, tabulation and scales
varieties.how: Match the basis of grouping: place = geographical, time = chronological, quality = qualitative, measured size = quantitative. For tables, captions are column heads and stubs are row heads.

example.q: Students of a college are grouped as "boys" and "girls". This is:
steps: Gender is a quality, not a measurement, so the classification is qualitative.
Only one attribute with two classes is used, so it is a simple (dichotomous) classification.

varieties.name: Class limits, boundaries, marks and widths
varieties.how: Class mark = (lower + upper) ÷ 2. For inclusive classes, half the gap between one upper limit and the next lower limit is taken off the lower limit and added to the upper limit.

example.q: For the inclusive classes 10–19, 20–29, 30–39, find the class boundaries, class width and class mark of 20–29.
steps: Gap between classes = 20 − 19 = 1, half of it = 0.5.

varieties.name: Bar diagrams and pie charts
varieties.how: Pie angle = (part ÷ total) × 360°. Each 1% of the total is 3.6°.

example.q: A family spends ₹2,400 a month, of which ₹360 goes on education. What is the angle for education in a pie chart?

varieties.name: Histogram, polygon and ogive
varieties.how: In a histogram the area shows the frequency, so for a wider class divide the frequency by (its width ÷ standard width). Ogives meet at the median.

example.q: Classes 0–10, 10–30 and 30–35 have frequencies 5, 16 and 6. Taking 10 as the standard width, find the heights of the histogram bars.

tips: Questionnaire is filled by the informant; schedule is filled by the enumerator. This pair is asked almost every year.
Class mark = average of the two limits. If the class marks are given, width = difference between two consecutive marks.
The less-than and more-than ogives cross at the median, so the x-value of the meeting point is the median.
For a pie chart, convert percentages with 1% = 3.6°: 20% = 72°, 25% = 90°, 50% = 180°.
For unequal classes in a histogram, adjust the frequency to the standard width before drawing; the area must match the frequency.
Sturges' rule: k = 1 + 3.322 log<sub>10</sub> N. Useful values: N = 100 gives about 8 classes, N = 1000 about 11.
traps: Inclusive classes (10–19) have different limits and boundaries; exclusive classes (10–20) do not.
A histogram uses class boundaries and touching bars; a bar diagram uses gaps between bars.
The less-than ogive uses upper boundaries; the more-than ogive uses lower boundaries.
Census data are primary for the Census office but secondary for anyone who later uses them.
Temperature in °C is an interval scale, not a ratio scale: 20 °C is not "twice as hot" as 10 °C.

formulas.name: Inclusive to exclusive
formulas.expr: subtract (gap ÷ 2) from lower limits and add it to upper limits

questions.q: The class mark of the class 20–30 is:
A list of questions that is filled in by the enumerator after asking the informant is called a:
questions.solution: A schedule is filled by the enumerator (as in the Population Census). A questionnaire is filled by the informant himself.

questions.q: A family spends ₹450 on food out of a total monthly expense of ₹1,800. In a pie chart, the angle for food is:
Using Sturges' rule, the number of classes for N = 1000 observations is about:
A frequency table has class 10–20 with f = 12 and class 20–40 with f = 30. Taking 10 as the standard width, the height of the histogram bar for 20–40 should be:
questions.solution:
Width of 20–40 is 20, which is 2 times the standard width 10.
Adjusted frequency = 30 × (10/20) = 15.

questions.q: For the inclusive classes 10–19, 20–29, 30–39, the upper class boundary of 20–29 is:
questions.solution:
Gap between classes = 20 − 19 = 1, half gap = 0.5.
Boundaries of 20–29 are 19.5 and 29.5, so the upper boundary is 29.5.
